title: “LOVE YOUR ENEMIES” — JESUS WASN’T TALKING ABOUT PEOPLE WHO MERELY ANNOY YOU
paragraphs:
“LOVE YOUR ENEMIES” — JESUS WASN’T TALKING ABOUT PEOPLE WHO MERELY ANNOY YOU
We made one of Jesus’ most terrifying commands sound sentimental. Then one day, somebody actually wounded us—and suddenly we discovered what He meant.
There is probably someone you would rather not think about while reading this.
Not the person who talks too loudly.
Not the coworker who irritates you.
Not the relative who posts things online that make you roll your eyes.
Someone deeper.
Someone whose name changes something inside you.
Maybe they betrayed you.
Maybe they humiliated you.
Maybe they lied about you while you stayed silent.
Maybe they abandoned you when you desperately needed them.
Maybe they smiled in your face while quietly destroying your reputation.
Maybe they took something from you that cannot simply be returned with an apology.
Maybe you trusted them with a vulnerable part of yourself...
and they used that knowledge as a weapon.
And if that person's face just appeared in your mind, then suddenly the words of Jesus do not sound like something printed on a Christian coffee mug.
They sound impossible.
“Love your enemies.”
We have heard those words so many times that familiarity has softened their blade.
But Jesus was not merely teaching Christians how to tolerate irritating personalities.
He was saying something far more disturbing.
And far more beautiful.
In Matthew 5:44, the Greek text reads:
ἀγαπᾶτε τοὺς ἐχθροὺς ὑμῶν καὶ προσεύχεσθε ὑπὲρ τῶν διωκόντων ὑμᾶς
Agapate tous echthrous hymōn kai proseuchesthe hyper tōn diōkontōn hymas.
In straightforward English:
Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you.
Look carefully at the word translated “enemies.”
ἐχθρούς — echthrous.
It carries the sense of enemies, hostile persons—people positioned against you.
Then notice what follows.
Jesus speaks about people persecuting His hearers.
Luke makes the uncomfortable meaning even harder to escape:
ἀγαπᾶτε τοὺς ἐχθροὺς ὑμῶν, καλῶς ποιεῖτε τοῖς μισοῦσιν ὑμᾶς
Agapate tous echthrous hymōn, kalōs poieite tois misousin hymas.
Love your enemies. Do good to those who hate you.
Not annoy you.
Hate you.
That changes everything.
Because Christianity becomes relatively easy when love is returned.
Love the people who love you.
Encourage the people who encourage you.
Invite the people who invite you.
Celebrate the people who celebrate you.
Give to the people who remember your birthday.
Forgive people whose offenses barely hurt.
Almost anybody can live like that.
Jesus Himself presses precisely this point in the Sermon on the Mount: if our love reaches only those who already love us, what is extraordinary about that?
Then Christ walks directly into the territory we desperately want to keep locked.
Love the person who became your enemy.
And suddenly Christianity stops being theoretical.
Because now you are remembering what they did.
The conversation.
The betrayal.
The screenshot.
The accusation.
The affair.
The abandonment.
The manipulation.
The money.
The lie.
The years you lost.
The night you cried where nobody could hear you.
And perhaps something inside you whispers:
“Jesus, You don't understand what they did to me.”
But then you remember where these words eventually lead.
To a cross.
Jesus did not preach enemy-love from the safety of a comfortable life and then disappear before experiencing hatred.
He lived it.
The One commanding enemy-love would Himself be rejected, mocked, falsely accused, beaten, crucified and publicly humiliated.
So Christianity never asks us to follow a Savior who remained untouched by human cruelty.
We follow the crucified Christ.
That matters enormously.
But we also need to understand what Jesus did not say.
Loving your enemy does not mean calling evil good.
It does not mean pretending betrayal did not happen.
It does not require describing abuse as acceptable.
It does not mean abandoning justice.
It does not mean refusing appropriate boundaries.
It does not necessarily mean restoring every broken relationship to its former intimacy.
Forgiveness and reconciliation are related, but they are not identical.
Forgiveness can refuse personal vengeance even when trust has been shattered. Reconciliation ordinarily requires truth, repentance and a rebuilding of trust.
You can forgive someone without handing them the same weapon again.
You can pray for someone from a distance.
You can refuse hatred while still telling the truth.
You can desire someone's redemption without allowing their destructive behavior unlimited access to your life.
Jesus does not command His followers to become accomplices to evil.
He commands something harder.
He forbids evil from becoming our master.
That is why Paul's words in Romans 12 are so important.
Do not repay evil for evil.
Do not avenge yourselves.
If your enemy is hungry, feed him.
If he is thirsty, give him something to drink.
And then comes the line that exposes the entire battle:
“Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.”
There it is.
The danger was never only what your enemy did to you.
The danger is what their sin might eventually produce inside you.
They wounded you...
and now bitterness wants to disciple you.
They lied...
and now revenge wants to preach to you.
They betrayed you...
and now hatred wants permission to move into your heart, rearrange the furniture and call itself justice.
That is the second wound.
And sometimes the second wound survives far longer than the first.
You can leave the person and still carry them everywhere.
They are sitting beside you at breakfast.
They are in the shower with you.
They appear when you lie down at night.
You replay imaginary conversations.
You compose speeches they will probably never hear.
You imagine the day everything collapses around them.
And occasionally, if we are painfully truthful, their suffering feels satisfying.
We may even dress that desire in religious language.
“God will deal with them.”
Perhaps He will.
God is just.
But sometimes what we secretly mean is:
“I hope God hurts them because I cannot.”
And Jesus reaches into that hidden room.
Not to shame the wounded.
To free them.
Because hatred creates a strange prison.
The person who injured you may no longer be anywhere near you...
yet they can still control your heartbeat.
A name appears and your peace disappears.
A photograph appears and your stomach tightens.
Someone mentions what happened and suddenly you are emotionally transported backward five years.
Ten years.
Twenty years.
The event ended.
But inside you, the trial never adjourned.
Every night your mind reconvenes court.
You present the evidence again.
You prosecute them again.
You sentence them again.
And somehow...
you keep serving the sentence.
This is where enemy-love begins to make sense.
Jesus is not asking you to pretend the wound was small.
He is asking you to surrender the throne.
“I will not become what hatred wants me to become.”
That is enemy-love.
“I will tell the truth, but I will not manufacture lies to destroy you.”
That is enemy-love.
“I may need distance, but I will not make revenge my god.”
That is enemy-love.
“I will not celebrate your destruction.”
That is enemy-love.
“I will pray that you encounter Jesus deeply enough to become someone different.”
That is enemy-love.
And perhaps that last one is the hardest.
Because praying for an enemy changes the prayer.
At first, maybe all you can manage is:
“Lord... You know.”
That may be where it starts.
Then perhaps:
“Lord, stop the evil.”
Then:
“Lord, bring the truth into the light.”
Then one day, trembling:
“Lord... save them.”
And that prayer can feel almost offensive.
Save them?
After what they did?
Yes.
Because that is precisely where the Gospel corners us.
We want grace for ourselves and justice for our enemies.
But at the cross, we discover that we ourselves came to God needing mercy.
Scripture does not divide humanity into innocent Christians and sinful enemies.
“All have sinned.”
Every Christian is a former rebel reconciled to God through Christ.
We did not negotiate our salvation.
We did not become sufficiently moral and force heaven to accept us.
Christ died for sinners.
Grace came looking for guilty people.
People like us.
That does not make every human offense identical. It does not minimize trauma, violence, betrayal or injustice.
It means something even more devastating:
The Gospel gives us no room to believe that another sinner is beyond the reach of the mercy that rescued us.
Think about that person again.
Yes.
That person.
What if Jesus transformed them?
Would you rejoice?
Do not answer quickly.
What if the person who wounded you fell to their knees before Christ tonight?
What if the Holy Spirit shattered their pride?
What if they confessed their sin?
What if they spent the rest of their life grieving what they had done and following Jesus?
What if you met them one day in eternity—not as the person who hurt you, but as a redeemed child of God washed by the same blood that washed you?
Would grace offend you?
That question exposes something.
Because sometimes we do not merely want justice.
We want ownership of the verdict.
But vengeance belongs to God.
And surrendering vengeance does not mean saying there will never be justice.
It means acknowledging that you are not God.
You can put down the gavel.
You can stop drinking poison while waiting for somebody else to die.
You can let the Judge judge.
And you can let the Savior save.
There is an astonishing Old Testament foundation beneath this teaching too.

Long before the Sermon on the Mount, Exodus instructed Israel that if someone encountered an enemy's wandering animal, he was to return it. If the animal belonging to someone who hated him collapsed under its burden, he was not simply to walk past.
Then Proverbs says that if your enemy is hungry, give him food; if he is thirsty, give him water.
Paul later draws directly from this wisdom in Romans 12.
The biblical trajectory is remarkably consistent.
God refuses to let His people use another person's hatred as permission to become hateful themselves.
Then Jesus brings the command into blazing clarity.
Love your enemies.
Do good.
Bless.
Pray.
Why?
Because this is what the family resemblance of heaven looks like.
God's children begin to resemble their Father.
And nowhere is that resemblance more shocking than when mercy appears where retaliation was expected.
The world understands revenge.
The world understands cancellation.
The world understands humiliation.
The world understands, “You hurt me, so I will hurt you harder.”
But when somebody has genuinely wronged you and discovers that they cannot turn you into another version of themselves...
something supernatural has happened.
Not weakness.
Freedom.
Jesus Christ has entered the wound.
And this is where the story becomes personal.
Maybe you have been asking God to remove your bitterness while secretly feeding it every morning.
Checking their profile.
Retelling the story.
Rehearsing the offense.
Finding new people who will confirm how terrible they are.
Keeping the wound open because healing almost feels like letting them get away with it.
But healing does not declare them innocent.
Healing declares that their sin will no longer own you.
There is a difference.
Maybe today your first act of enemy-love is not calling them.
Maybe calling them would be unwise.
Maybe reconciliation is currently impossible.
Maybe authorities, counselors, pastors, courts or protective boundaries appropriately belong in your situation.
Your first act may simply happen behind a closed door where nobody sees you.
You whisper their name before God.
Your jaw tightens.
Your eyes fill.
Everything inside you resists.
And you say:
“Jesus... I give You my right to revenge.”
Maybe you cannot yet say, “I feel love for them.”
Jesus never said you had to manufacture warm feelings.
Biblical love is bigger than emotional affection.
So perhaps you pray:

“Lord, I don't know how to do this. But I refuse to worship my hatred. Give me the grace to desire what You desire. Protect people from evil. Bring truth into the light. Bring justice where justice is needed. And if this person can be redeemed... redeem them.”
That prayer may cost you something.
Pray it anyway.
Because the scandal of Christianity is not that good people receive trophies.
The scandal is grace.
Grace for Peter after denial.
Grace for persecutors who repent.
Grace for thieves.
Grace for prodigals.
Grace for the sexually broken.
Grace for religious hypocrites who finally fall before God.
Grace for you.
Grace for me.
Grace purchased not with sentimental optimism, but with the blood of Jesus Christ.
And this is why the cross stands at the center of everything.
At Calvary, God did not shrug at sin.
Sin was so serious that Christ bore judgment.
And God's mercy was so astonishing that the Son willingly gave Himself to save sinners.
Justice was not treated as meaningless.
Grace was not cheapened.
Christ was crucified.
Then the grave opened.
That is why Christians can relinquish personal vengeance.
Our hope is not that evil does not matter.
Our hope is that God is Judge...
and Jesus is Savior.
So perhaps the real question is no longer:
“Do they deserve my forgiveness?”
Maybe the deeper question is:
“What did I deserve when Jesus came for me?”
That one hurts.
Because suddenly we are standing on level ground beneath the cross.
Still wounded.
Still telling the truth.
Still perhaps maintaining necessary boundaries.
But no longer pretending grace belongs exclusively to people whose sins we find tolerable.
This is where scandals become testimonies.
This is where wounds stop writing the ending.
This is where Jesus takes a story that should have produced another bitter human being and writes something nobody expected.
Mercy.
Freedom.
Healing.
Holiness.
A heart that remembers what happened without needing revenge to survive.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
If this exposed a name you have been trying not to remember, do not rush past it.
Sit with Christ.
Be honest.
Somebody reading silently may desperately need evidence that freedom is possible.
Not because every word will feel comfortable today.
Not as a performance of spirituality.
Not because an algorithm is sacred.
Because a person is.
Somebody you know may be smiling publicly while privately rehearsing revenge against someone who shattered them.
Put truth where they can find it.
And if that somebody is you...
hear this before you leave:
You do not have to call evil good.
You do not have to pretend it never happened.
You do not have to restore unsafe access.
You do not have to manufacture feelings you do not possess.
But because of Jesus, you no longer have to let hatred finish the story your enemy started.
Lay down the gavel.
Give the wound to Christ.
Pray the impossible prayer.
And remember this:
The deepest victory over your enemy may not be watching God destroy them—it may be watching Jesus finally remove them from the throne they have occupied inside your heart.
